problem: The lift relation is wrong. After the roll, the lift plane contains the commanded acceleration vector, so the wing must produce the full command magnitude a_total, not a_total cos φ. The quantity a_total cos φ is only the in-plane component of the command before rolling (equal to √(a_total² − a_side²)); it is not the lift. As written the example is physically impossible: the missile is said to accelerate at 8 g while the wing gives only 6.93 g, and nothing supplies the remaining 4 g sideways component. The same slip makes Exam trap 2 and Quiz Q3 answers wrong.
fix: Use a_L = a_total after the roll. State that the command has an in-plane part a_in = a_total cos φ and a sideways part a_side = a_total sin φ before rolling; the roll by φ puts both into the lift plane, so the lift equals a_total. Worked example: φ = asin(4/8) = 30.0° and the wing must give 8 g (about 78.5 m/s²) of lift; the in-plane component before rolling was 6.93 g. Quiz Q3: φ = 30.0° and a_L = 6 g, not 5.20 g. Exam trap 2 should read: after the roll the lift is the full command a_total; its components along the old lift plane and across it are a_total cos φ and a_total sin φ.

problem: A dynamically tuned gyro does have a spinning rotor (spun by a small motor); only the ring laser gyro and the fibre optic gyro have no spinning mass. The sentence wrongly groups all three as mass-free.
fix: Write: 'Modern missiles use ring laser or fibre optic gyros, which have no spinning mass and low drift; dynamically tuned gyros, which do have a small spinning rotor, are also used.'

problem: Accelerations are quoted in g but g is never defined, while the rest of the chapter uses m/s².
fix: Add: 'g is the acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s², so 8 g = 78.5 m/s².'
